note: Faculty-facing summaries per (strand, age band). Every topic appears in exactly one cluster.

clusters.subject: Ethics & Provenance
clusters.name: First questions of fairness
clusters.summary: These four are the youngest students' first brush with the ethics that later runs through the whole programme. They learn that a machine's bias comes straight from its examples, that running AI spends real energy and water, and that their own data has value someone else collects. One node teaches that hard ethical calls have no single right answer, only sides you can weigh. Keep these as conversations, not verdicts. The aim is to plant the questions early, so the studio years have somewhere to land.

clusters.subject: Foundations
clusters.name: What a machine actually is
clusters.summary: This is the on-ramp: the youngest students meeting AI before they ever open a design tool. They learn that AI already picks what reaches their eyes, that it learns from examples rather than written rules, and that to a computer a photo is just data. Two nodes build the thinking underneath — chance on a scale from impossible to certain, and the gap between what a text says and what you assumed. None of it is architecture yet. It is the plain, honest ground the later years stand on.

clusters.subject: Generative Mechanics
clusters.name: The coordinate sense
clusters.summary: A single on-ramp node, but it earns its place. Before a student can grasp embeddings or latent space in the studio years, they need the plain intuition that two numbers pin a point on a grid, and that points sitting close together are close in meaning. Here they get it through ordinary coordinate geometry — plotting a point, then sliding and turning a shape without changing what it is. It looks like a maths lesson, and at eleven to fifteen that is exactly what it should be. The pay-off comes years later, when "meaning as coordinates" stops being a metaphor.

clusters.subject: Judgment
clusters.name: The first habits of judgment
clusters.summary: Judgment starts young, long before there is a render to critique. These four teach the youngest students to check a source before trusting an image, to read a whole set of data instead of one point, and to change one thing at a time so they know what caused the difference. One node names the mental shortcuts that quietly skew a choice. Nothing here mentions AI images directly. It is the disposition — sceptical, careful, one variable at a time — that the studio crit will later demand.

clusters.subject: Studio Practice
clusters.name: Reading before building
clusters.summary: Before a student runs a single studio workflow, they need the reading habits underneath it. These three teach the youngest to tell a checkable fact from a writer's opinion, to weigh where an answer came from, and to treat a claim as only as good as its evidence — and to update when better evidence arrives. It is research hygiene at its plainest. There is no AI tool in sight yet. But every "verify before you build on it" rule in the studio years grows straight out of these.

clusters.subject: The Brief
clusters.name: The words come first
clusters.summary: The brief begins with language and proportion, long before it meets a prompt. These three teach the youngest students that a drawing keeps its shape only if every part scales together, that the same message is written differently for a different reader, and that the exact word does real work "nice" cannot. It is vocabulary and ratio treated as tools, not decoration. There is no AI here yet. But a student who cannot name what they mean will never brief a machine to make it.

clusters.subject: Ethics & Provenance
clusters.name: Provenance and the honest submission
clusters.summary: This is where a student learns that the tool they just opened was trained on other people's work, mostly without asking. From there it turns concrete for a design school: what counts as plagiarism now, what must be declared in a submission, and what a free tool quietly takes from them and their client. These are the habits that keep a portfolio honest before the stakes get high. The register is factual — each claim anchored to a source, not to an opinion. Teach it as citation discipline, not as a lecture on morals.

clusters.subject: Foundations
clusters.name: How the machine really works
clusters.summary: This is the largest foundation region, and it earns its size: everything downstream rests on it. Students learn that a model predicts rather than understands, that its whole world is its training data, and that a confident answer and a correct one are not the same thing. They meet the parts of a chatbot, the closed world behind the training cutoff, and the difference between finding something and inventing it. Two positional nodes set the stakes — why AI differs in kind from CAD, and why building this literacy from an under-photographed India is representation, not catch-up. Get this layer wrong and every later judgment is built on sand.

clusters.subject: Generative Mechanics
clusters.name: Inside the engine
clusters.summary: This is where the black box gets opened. Students see how words and images become numbers, how diffusion pulls a picture out of noise, and why a language model is only ever guessing the next token. They learn the engine families — the dreaming ones that invent and the grounded ones held to real inputs — plus attention, the context window, and why the same prompt never lands twice. The whole region is factual, each idea anchored to an essay and a source, because these are mechanics, not opinions. Once a student understands the machine this well, "it glitched" stops being an acceptable thing to say in crit.

clusters.subject: The Brief
clusters.name: The prompt is a brief
clusters.summary: This region makes one provocative claim and builds everything on it: a prompt is not a wish, it is a brief you hand a machine, and briefing is the oldest skill in practice aimed at the newest tool. Students learn the precise words for space, material, and light, the difference between style words that return the average and substance words that return their building, and the seven slots a complete visual brief must fill. Several nodes are positional — naming intent over deliverable, setting criteria before generating, matching a different register to each engine family. Any slot they leave blank, the model fills with its own default. Assess the brief, not just the image it produced.

clusters.subject: Ethics & Provenance
clusters.name: Ethics with real consequences
clusters.summary: By now ethics stops being a discussion and starts having consequences a client can feel. Students face the tilted default that draws every house American, the render that lies about a site, the licence that decides whether an image can be sold, and the craft tradition a prompt strips for free. The hardest nodes are positional: they ask the student to take an authored stand — name the flattening, refuse to ship the placeless image, disclose before a jury asks. Others stay factual, anchored to what data centres, annotators, and scraped datasets actually cost. This is the layer where authorship, provenance, and refusal become professional reflexes, defended out loud rather than filed away.

clusters.subject: Generative Mechanics
clusters.name: From engine to studio system
clusters.summary: Now the mechanics turn into decisions a practice actually makes. Students learn the controls that steer a grounded generation, how retrieval feeds a model a studio's own archive, and how tools and agents let a model reach past text into a real workflow. The judgment nodes are the point: fine-tune or retrieve, open weights or API, and how to evaluate a model on your own work instead of a leaderboard. A positional thread runs through it — that retrieval usually beats a bigger context window, and that a studio's memory problem is really a retrieval problem. This is the bridge from understanding the engine to building a system around it.

clusters.subject: Judgment
clusters.name: The crit wall
clusters.summary: This is the heart of the whole taxonomy, and it is almost entirely positional. Students stop treating AI images as answers and start treating them as evidence to cross-examine: reading a batch like a contact sheet, telling variation from real difference, and finding the load path that isn't there. They learn that fifty images is gambling, that the red pen is where authorship lives, and that the sharpest move is sometimes refusing to generate at all. Mastery here is shown at the crit wall, not in a quiz — a student defends the chain of decisions behind an image, not the image itself. If a node in this region were graded by a written test, the assessment would have missed the point.

clusters.subject: Studio Practice
clusters.name: AI across the whole practice
clusters.summary: This is the biggest studio region, and it carries the programme's payoff: AI placed across a real project, from site research to handover, always under a judgment the student can state. They learn to map a workflow before adding AI, to route a task to the right kind of engine, to verify every claim against a primary source, and to keep files a stranger — or an agent — could navigate. The positional spine is blunt: reduce friction, not judgment; the deliberate "no" is a design decision; and the capstone is one full project where every AI step traces back to a choice the student made. Assess it the way you assess a thesis — by whether they can account for the whole thread, out loud. A good-looking image proves nothing here.

clusters.subject: The Brief
clusters.name: Briefing as authored practice
clusters.summary: In the studio years the brief becomes a working document with a life of its own. Students decode a messy client brief down to its drivers, then run it backwards — generating a full brief from three vague lines and red-penning it as its editor. They learn the six-layer reasoning brief, the brief kept in versions as a record of thinking, and the loop where a crit rewrites the brief instead of just re-rolling the image. The stance is clear: generation is a first draft of thinking, and editing is where authorship lives. A brief a stranger can find and reuse six months later is the mark of the mature user.
